html:
A huge inscription and relief carved about 520 BCE on a cliff of Mount Behistun in western Iran, on the old road from Babylon to the Median capital Ecbatana. In it Darius the Great tells how he took the throne and beat the rebels who rose against him.

The relief shows Darius with his foot on a fallen rival and nine captive rebel kings roped together before him. The text repeats the same story in three languages, all in cuneiform: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Copies were sent across the Achaemenid Empire.

The British officer Henry Rawlinson copied the text between 1835 and the late 1840s, climbing ropes and ladders to reach it. Old Persian was deciphered first, and with it as a key scholars cracked Babylonian Akkadian, opening up the written record of Mesopotamia. Behistun did for cuneiform what the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian hieroglyphs.
